item.title: The write lock is not your problem
item.description: WAL and a single serialized writer.
item.content:encoded:
SQLite permits many readers and exactly one writer.

Everything that follows is padding with a purpose: it makes this article taller than a browser window, which is the only way the reading pane becomes something a reader can travel through.

A journal is a sequence of frames appended to a file. The database itself is not modified while a transaction runs.

Readers see the database as it was when they began, plus whatever frames the journal has committed since.

A checkpoint folds those frames back into the main file. Until it runs, the file on disk is behind and that is not a problem.

Two connections, one for reading and one for writing, keep the two workloads from arguing with each other about a mutex.

The writer is serialized because there is exactly one of it, not because anything queues.

A busy timeout turns an immediate failure into a short wait, which is almost always what the caller wanted.

Synchronous NORMAL trades a fsync per commit for a fsync per checkpoint, and on a journal that is a safe trade.

Foreign keys are off by default, which makes every REFERENCES clause decorative until something turns them on.

None of this is visible from the application, and that is the measure of whether it was done correctly.

The failure mode worth rehearsing is the one where a copy is taken while frames are still outstanding.

Such a copy opens cleanly, passes a smoke test, and is missing whatever had not been folded back in yet.

That is why a copy is taken through the database rather than through the filesystem.

And that is the end of the padding.
